title: Platformization
text:
Measures
Video format was coded using zero-shot classification with multimodal LLMs using video frames. Emoji use was measured using the emo_detect() function from the {emoji} package (Hvitfeldt 2024). Audience interactions were coded using zero-shot classification with multimodal LLMs using post text, transcript and video frames.






Coding instructions





Your task is to analyze the provided short video content based on the provided video frames, text and transcript. Do not infer beyond what you can directly observe in the text or images. Please evaluate the provided video content against each of the following 4 characteristics independently:
direct_audience_address: Code “True” if the narrator speaks directly to the viewer or the text addresses the audience using direct pronouns or imperatives (e.g., “Have you heard?”, “You need to see this,” or a person pointing at the camera). Code “False” if the content is purely observational or third-person reporting.
community_mentions: Code “True” if the video, caption, or transcript mentions specific audience members, usernames, or community feedback. This includes “Replying to (user?),” screenshots of comments, or phrases like “You guys have been asking” or “In the comments, people said.” Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_like: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to “like,” “heart,” “save,” “bookmark,” or “upvote” (e.g., “Double tap if you agree,” “Save this for later”). Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_comment_discuss: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to write a comment, answer a specific question, or engage in a discussion (e.g., “Tell us your thoughts,” “What do you think?”). Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_share: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to share the video, send it to others, or repost it to a story/feed. Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_follow_subscribe: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to follow the account, subscribe to the channel, or visit the profile/page for more content (e.g., “Hit the plus sign,” “Follow for more”). Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_website_app: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to visit the outlet’s own digital products, such as a website for a full article or an app (e.g., “Link in bio,” “Read the full story on our site”). Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_traditional_media: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to consume the outlet’s traditional media, such as watching a TV broadcast, listening to a radio show, or reading a print edition (e.g., “Watch the full report tonight on [Channel Name]”). Code “False” otherwise.
call_to_social_platform: Code “True” if there is a verbal or visual prompt to visit the outlet on a specifically mentioned social media platform (e.g., “Check our YouTube,” “Live updates on our Twitter”). Code “False” otherwise.

title: Platform News Report
text:
Platformization describes the growing trend of news being produced and distributed through – and increasingly by – digital platforms like TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram. This process fundamentally alters news production, often prioritizing engagement over traditional journalistic norms. Consequently, platform news are supposedly more visually-driven, emotionalized, and personalized, often delivered by non-traditional actors and in new formats.
To systematically investigate these shifts, we introduce the Platform News Report, a large-scale computational communication research project examining news content on TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram.
Complementing the Reuters Digital News Report, which primarily focuses on survey data and news consumption patterns, our study examines the content and dissemination of news on these platforms. Our sampling scheme directly aligns with the DNR, leveraging the same markets and covering the news brands. This parallel approach ensures comparability and allows for a more holistic understanding of the news ecosystem, bridging insights from both demand and supply sides.
The project collects data from 571 news outlets across 46 countries, enabling analysis of the topics covered, the presentation styles employed, and the patterns of publication on these platforms. Through this comprehensive dataset, the Platform News Report aims to provide empirical insights into the evolving landscape of digital news and the consequences of platformization for public discourse.






Work-in-progress



The Platform News Report is work-in-progress, and we actively encourage engagement from the research community and beyond. We welcome suggestions for improvement, new analyses, comments on preliminary findings, and – crucially – bug reports to help ensure the accuracy and robustness of our data and analyses.



Team
The Platform News Report is a project of the Computational Communication Research Group at the Department of Communication, Johannes-Gutenberg University Mainz, Germany.
Principle investigator: Michael Scharkow
Research assistance: Yannick Winkler, Dennis Maus, Charlotte Tryba


Citation
Please cite as Scharkow, Michael (2025). Platform News Report 2025. Online at https://ccsmainz.github.io/platformnews

title: News topics
text:
Overview
We analyzed the topics of the posts by using zero-shot classification of the post title and transcript. Based on the topic list from the Electronic News Archive (ENA) of the University of Antwerp, we coded the presence of 19 from politics to sports, with a few platform-specific additions like user-generated performances, which includes typical dance and lip sync videos, or advertisements and promotions.
Perhaps surprisingly, “hard news” topics like politics and crime dominate, while typical platform content is relatively rarely published by news outlets.

title: News topics
text:
Topic details
In the subsections below, we provide detailed information about all coded news topics, along with comparisons by platform, media type and country.

Politics
Across all analyzed short video posts, we found that an average of 27% covered politics. When examining differences by platform, we observed that posts on Instagram were slightly more likely to cover political topics at 30% compared to 25% on TikTok, a statistically significant distinction, while YouTube Shorts posts, at 29%, were similar to Instagram. Outlet type also played a role, with public broadcasters dedicating significantly less of their short video content to politics, averaging 23%, a notable contrast to digital outlets, print media, and private broadcasters, all of which had a higher and similar share around 30%. Furthermore, we identified substantial variation across countries; for instance, Poland stood out with nearly half of its short video posts (49%) covering politics, whereas countries like Belgium, Croatia, and Norway presented a much lower proportion, around 16%.

Topic: Politics by platformby outlet typeby country






































Law enforcement and crime
We found that 26% of short video posts, on average, covered law enforcement and crime. When examining differences by platform, we observed that the share of posts ranged narrowly from 25% on Instagram and YouTube Shorts to 27% on TikTok, but these differences were small and not statistically significant based on the provided analysis. Similarly, differences across outlet types were also small and not statistically significant, with digital outlets covering law enforcement and crime in 22% of posts, print outlets in 24%, public broadcasters in 27%, and private broadcasters in 28%. However, we identified substantial variation across countries, with the share of posts ranging from a low of 18% in Romania to a high of 40% in Peru. Other countries with high coverage included Mexico (35%), South Africa (34%), and Turkey (34%), while Hungary (19%) and Croatia (19%) showed some of the lowest shares alongside Romania.

Topic: Law by platformby outlet typeby country






































War disasters accidents
Across all analyzed short video posts, we found that war, disasters, and accidents constituted an average of 23% of the content. Looking at differences by platform, we observed that YouTube Shorts dedicated a notably higher share to these topics, at 28%, compared to TikTok’s 23% and Instagram’s 21%; specifically, posts on YouTube Shorts featured war, disaster, and accident content 6 percentage points more often than on TikTok. Outlet types also showed significant variations: public broadcasters covered these topics most frequently, at 30%, which was 12 percentage points higher than digital outlets, which had the lowest share at 18%. Print and private broadcasters had similar coverage levels, around 20%. Finally, we found considerable differences across countries, with the share of posts on war, disasters, and accidents ranging from a low of 18% in countries like Brazil and the Czech Republic to a high of 29% in Australia.

Topic: War by platformby outlet typeby country






































Economy and finance
We observed that an average of 17% of short video posts across all analyzed platforms and outlets covered economy and finance. However, we found that this share varied significantly by platform: posts on TikTok were more likely to cover these topics, at 19%, compared to Instagram, where only 13% of posts did, a difference of 6 percentage points. YouTube Shorts fell in between, with 17% of posts focusing on economy and finance. When examining outlet types, we found only small and non-significant differences, with digital and print outlets posting about economy and finance in approximately 15% of their videos, while private and public broadcasters did so in 17% and 18% of their videos, respectively. Finally, we saw a broader range of coverage across countries, from a low of 13% in the Czech Republic to a high of 20% in Mexico.

Topic: Economy by platformby outlet typeby country






































Social affairs
We found that, across all observed short video posts, an average of 21% covered social affairs. Regarding platforms, TikTok posts featured social affairs content at a slightly higher rate of 23%, while Instagram and YouTube Shorts showed smaller shares, both at 18%. When examining different outlet types, public broadcasters stood out, dedicating a substantially larger share of their posts to social affairs at 27%, which was an 8 percentage point higher share than digital outlets, for example, which covered social affairs in 16% of their posts. Print and private broadcasters showed similar shares to digital outlets, ranging from 17% to 18%. Finally, the coverage of social affairs varied considerably by country, ranging from a low of 13% in Taiwan, and around 15% in countries like Brazil, Chile, and Greece, to a high of 29% in Nigeria, with other nations such as Germany, Ireland, and South Africa also featuring higher proportions of social affairs content (around 25-26%).

Topic: Social by platformby outlet typeby country






































Health and fitness
We found that across all short video posts analyzed, an average of 9% covered health and fitness topics. When we examined the distribution of this content across different platforms, such as TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube Shorts, we observed that the share of health and fitness posts remained consistently around 9% to 10%, with no statistically significant differences identified between them. Similarly, when we explored variations by outlet type, including digital, print, private broadcaster, and public broadcaster, the proportion of health and fitness content ranged narrowly from 7% to 10%, and these differences were also found to be small and not statistically significant. Lastly, our analysis across various countries revealed that the coverage of health and fitness content in short videos generally hovered between 8% and 10%, with no statistically significant variations noted across the individual nations studied.

Topic: Health by platformby outlet typeby country






































Mobility and infrastructure
We found that across all short video posts analyzed, the share covering mobility and infrastructure was, on average, 7%. When examining specific platforms, we observed only small and statistically non-significant variations in this coverage; posts on TikTok dedicated approximately 6% to these topics, Instagram posts about 7%, and YouTube Shorts posts roughly 8%. Similarly, the outlet type—whether digital, print, private broadcaster, or public broadcaster—did not significantly influence the proportion of mobility and infrastructure content, with all types hovering around 7%. Furthermore, we found no substantial differences in the share of these posts when comparing across individual countries, with the majority of nations showing a 7% share, and a few, such as Brazil and Romania, exhibiting a slightly lower, though not statistically distinct, 6%.

Environment and energy
Overall, we found that 5% of short video posts covered environment and energy topics. When examining differences across platforms, we observed that YouTube Shorts posts were more likely to cover these topics (at 7%) compared to Instagram posts (4%), while TikTok posts showed an intermediate share of 5%. Regarding outlet types, public broadcasters dedicated a notably higher share of their posts to environment and energy (6%) compared to private broadcasters (3%); the shares for digital and print outlets were both 4%, and these differences were small and not consistently distinct from other categories. Country-level variations also emerged, with the share of posts covering these topics ranging from 3% in countries like the Czech Republic and Romania, to 6% in countries such as Australia, Nigeria, Singapore, and South Africa.

Topic: Environment by platformby outlet typeby country






































Science technology and education
We found that, on average, approximately 8% of short video posts covered science, technology, and education. This share varied significantly across platforms and outlet types. Looking at platforms, YouTube Shorts dedicated the largest share of its content to these topics at 12%, which was substantially higher than TikTok, where only 7% of posts covered science, technology, and education. Instagram posts for this category were around 8%. When examining outlet types, public broadcasters were notable for featuring science, technology, and education content in 12% of their posts, a significantly higher proportion compared to digital outlets, which allocated 6% of their content to these areas. Private broadcasters and print outlets showed similar, lower shares, at 7% and 5% respectively. We also observed variability across countries, with the share of science, technology, and education posts ranging from a low of 5% in countries like Brazil and Denmark to a high of 11% in Singapore, and 10% in several others, including Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

For outlet types, we found only small and non-significant differences in the proportion of culture and arts posts, which ranged from 4% for private broadcasters to 7% for print outlets. Finally, the share of culture and arts posts varied across countries, ranging from a low of 3% in South Korea to a high of 8% in Morocco.

Overall, we found that lifestyle and travel content constituted a relatively small portion of short video posts, averaging 7%. When examining differences across platforms, we observed that TikTok had a significantly higher share of such content, featuring lifestyle and travel in 8% of posts, compared to YouTube Shorts at 4%, a difference of 4 percentage points. Instagram posts featured lifestyle and travel content in 7% of cases, but this difference was not statistically significant compared to other platforms based on the available contrasts. Differences by outlet type were small and not statistically significant; digital and print outlets showed shares of 9% and 8% respectively, while private and public broadcasters both had 6%. Similarly, while the share of lifestyle and travel content varied by country, ranging from 5% in South Korea to 9% in Denmark, these differences were generally small and not statistically significant across countries.

Fashion and beauty
On average, we found that 2% of all short video posts covered fashion and beauty. The prevalence of this content varied significantly across platforms: TikTok stood out with 3% of its posts dedicated to fashion and beauty, which was notably higher than Instagram and YouTube Shorts, where only 1% of posts featured such topics. We also observed statistically significant differences across outlet types: private and public broadcasters both had 2% of their posts covering fashion and beauty, which was double the 1% observed for print outlets; digital outlets similarly had 1% of posts, but this estimate was not as robustly supported by the data. Across countries, however, the share of fashion and beauty content remained consistently low, ranging between 1% and 2%, with no large or substantially meaningful variations observed.

We found that, on average, short video posts dedicated to food and cooking represented 3% of all content. When examining this across platforms, we observed only small and statistically non-significant differences; for instance, YouTube Shorts had a predicted share of 4%, while TikTok and Instagram both had 3%. Outlet type, however, showed a notable distinction: digital, print, and private broadcasters each allocated approximately 4% of their posts to food and cooking, whereas public broadcasters covered these topics significantly less often, at just 1%. Across all analyzed short video posts, we found that content related to pets and animals constituted, on average, a share of 3% of all posts. Measures
Topics were coded using using zero-short classification on post text and transcript, with categories from the Electronic News Archive (ENA) of the University of Antwerp and additional topics.






Coding instructions





Your task is to analyze the provided short video content (derived from caption text and transcripts) and determine whether its topic explicitly falls into one or more of the following categories. Your decision for each category must be based only on direct and explicit mentions of the category’s subject matter within the caption text or transcript. Do not infer or extrapolate beyond the directly stated information. If a category’s subject is not explicitly mentioned, even if indirectly related, you must classify it as “False.”
Please evaluate the provided short video content against each of the following 19 categories independently:
politics: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly discusses political structures, electoral processes, or international governance. This includes explicit mentions of political organizations, elections, migration policies, and international relations between countries.
law_enforcement_and_crime: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly deals with the legal system, law enforcement activities, or criminal acts. This includes explicit mentions of the judiciary, crime policy, specific instances of crime, and civil rights and freedoms.
war_disasters_accidents: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly reports on armed conflicts, defense matters, or major calamitous events. This includes explicit discussions of war and peace, weaponry, and natural or man-made disasters and accidents.
economy_and_finance: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly focuses on economic activity, financial markets, or labor. This includes explicit mentions of finance (e.g., banking, stock markets), the general economy, consumer affairs, and labor issues like employment or wages.
social_affairs: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly is centered on broad societal issues and demographic trends. This includes explicit mentions of social policies like healthcare, social security, and housing, as well as population growth or aging.
health_and_fitness: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly focuses on personal health, medical conditions, physical fitness, or wellness. This includes explicit mentions of diet, exercise, mental health, and general medical advice, distinct from healthcare policy.
mobility_and_infrastructure: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly discusses transportation systems or public works. This includes explicit mentions of mobility, traffic, and spatial planning, such as urban development or infrastructure projects.
environment_and_energy: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly concerns the natural world, energy resources, or food production. This includes explicit mentions of environmental protection, nature conservation, energy policy, and agriculture.
science_technology_and_education: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly is about scientific research, technological advancements, or education systems. This includes explicit mentions of cultural patrimony, the education sector, aerospace exploration, and telecommunication.
culture_and_arts: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly focuses on creative and fine arts or matters of faith. This includes explicit mentions of performing arts (e.g., theater, dance), literature, visual arts (e.g., painting), and religion.
lifestyle_and_travel: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly covers personal interests, leisure activities, travel, or daily routines. This includes explicit mentions of general lifestyle topics (e.g., hobbies), tourism, personal vlogs, and “day-in-the-life” content.
fashion_and_beauty: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly focuses on clothing, accessories, personal style, makeup, skincare, or cosmetic products. This includes explicit mentions of fashion hauls, outfit styling, makeup tutorials, and product reviews within these areas.
food_and_cooking: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly discusses recipes, cooking techniques, food preparation, dining experiences, food reviews, or specific food items. This includes explicit mentions of quick meals, baking, restaurant reviews, and food-related challenges.
pets_and_animals: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly features or discusses domestic pets, wild animals, animal behavior, or animal care, with the primary focus being the animal itself.
entertainment_news_and_industry: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly discusses news, releases, reviews, or industry aspects related to professional film, television, or music. This includes explicit mentions of movie releases, album launches, TV show reviews, film festivals, and the business operations of traditional media companies.
celebrity: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly focuses on the personal lives, private relationships, or non-professional activities of famous individuals. For any famous individual (e.g., politician, athlete, pop star, royals), code “True” only if the content explicitly concerns their personal life or non-professional activities. Otherwise, their professional activities should only be classified under the relevant category such as politics, sports, etc. Attention: Simply mentioning a famous person, e.g. a president or queen, is not sufficient for a post being coded as “True” celebrity news.
sports: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly is about sports as a field of activity. This includes explicit coverage of sporting events, competitions, games, teams, and the professional performance of sports athletes.
promotion_and_advertisements: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly promotes a product, service, brand, event, or specific call to action with a commercial intent. This includes explicit mentions of sales, discounts, sponsorships, brand endorsements, or direct calls to purchase or visit a business.
user_generated_performance_and_comedy: Code “True” if the caption text or transcript explicitly features or discusses performances by users, often for entertainment, and/or comedic content. This includes explicit mentions of dance routines, lip-sync videos, short-form skits, memes, and viral trends where a user’s performance or comedic element is central.

title: About the project
text: This research project conducts a supply-side analysis of news content on social media platforms, including TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube Shorts. Complementing the Reuters Digital News Report, which primarily focuses on survey data and news consumption patterns, our study examines the content and dissemination of news on these platforms. We investigate the characteristics of news content, analyzing its styles, formats, and publication patterns. By focusing on the strategies and content production from news organizations and creators, this project aims to provide an understanding of how news is presented within the evolving landscape of short-form video and visual-first platforms.

Content duplication
Our analysis revealed that 17% of short video posts were cross-platform duplicates on average. When examining differences by platform, we found that YouTube Shorts had a significantly higher share of duplicated content at 21%, compared to 16% on both TikTok and Instagram. This represents a 6 percentage point increase for YouTube Shorts over TikTok. Looking at outlet types, public broadcasters duplicated content most frequently, with 26% of their posts being duplicates. This was substantially higher than digital outlets, which showed the lowest duplication at 12%, while print and private broadcasters had similar duplication rates of 16%. We also observed considerable variation across countries; for instance, Australia and Ireland showed the highest rates of content duplication, both at 59%, whereas countries like Greece, Morocco, and Taiwan had the lowest rates, with only 2% of their posts being duplicates.
